dtz.lead: Most people who apply for Spanish nationality by residence must show Spanish at A2 or higher and pass the CCSE. Here you can read about DELE A2 and practise with our own mock.
dtz.who.title: Who is this for?
dtz.who.text: DELE A2 is the Instituto Cervantes diploma at level A2. Most applicants for nationality by residence need it, or a higher DELE, together with the CCSE. Some people are exempt from one or both: nationals of Spanish-speaking countries, for example, usually don't need the DELE. The rules can change, so check the official sources before you book. This is general orientation, not legal advice.
dtz.format.note: This is the structure of our own mock, not of the real exam. For the real parts and timings, as far as we could check them, see our DELE A2 practice set and the Instituto Cervantes. The mock has no speaking part: practise that with our speaking tasks. The extra reading & writing tasks are good for more practice.
dtz.scoring.title: How DELE A2 is marked
dtz.scoring.text: The final result of a DELE is pass or fail (apto or no apto). The parts are scored in groups, and the Instituto Cervantes publishes the current rule. In our mock the point bands are our own guide, not a DELE score.
dtz.set.title: Our DELE A2 mock: listening, reading and writing
dtz.set.text: Nine parts, 45 scored tasks in Spanish at level A2: listening parts 1–4 and reading parts 1–5, plus a writing task with a model answer. You can run a clock for each skill. At the end you see your result by part, with our own point bands as a guide. Progress stays saved in the browser.

dtz.mock.text: All four reading tasks as one continuous test at level B1, a step above DELE A2, with an overall result at the end.
dtz.practice.intro: These practice tools train the skills that DELE A2 tests.
telc.lead: The tasks of the SIELE, one band at a time. The real exam climbs from A1 to C1 in one sitting; here you can practise the tasks that aim at your level, and the four sets together hold one whole exam.
telc.who.title: Who is SIELE for?
telc.who.text: SIELE is one exam for all levels rather than one exam per level. There is no pass mark: each test gives you a score and a CEFR level. People take it for study and work, and whether it is accepted depends on the institution, so check before you book. It doesn't count for Spanish nationality, according to the SIELE site: that route needs the DELE at A2 or above, plus the CCSE.
telc.sprachbausteine.note: SIELE has four tests and no separate grammar paper. Grammar, vocabulary and cohesion are tested in context, in the 12-gap text of reading task 5.
telc.moreLevels.title: How this differs from the real exam
telc.moreLevels.text: The bands are our way of cutting up one exam: you can't book a "SIELE B1". Task types, numbers of questions and word counts follow the public exam guide, which may be some years old, and our times are our own share of the real test time. Check the current details on siele.org. The whole exam, its scores and its options are on the SIELE page.

goethe.lead: The official Spanish diplomas of the Instituto Cervantes, recognised by employers, universities and public bodies.
goethe.who.title: Who is the DELE for?
goethe.who.text: Each DELE diploma is a separate exam for one level, from A1 to C2. People use it for work, for study and, usually at A2 or above, for Spanish nationality. As far as we could check, a DELE diploma has no expiry date, though some institutions may ask for a recent result.
goethe.modell.title: Official sample tests
goethe.moreLevels.text: The Instituto Cervantes publishes sample papers (modelos de examen) for the DELE. We do not copy them. The formats above come from public exam information, checked on 6 November 2026. Its centres' pages do not all agree on every detail, so read the current exam guide before you book.
goethe.a1.title: A1: our own practice test
goethe.a1.text: Our A1 practice test follows the general shape of the DELE A1, with listening, reading, writing and speaking. It is shorter than the real exam and not official, and its 60 % pass line is our own convention.

testdaf.lead: The computer-based Spanish test for levels A1 to C1. Each test gets a score from 0 to 250 and a CEFR level. There is no pass mark.
testdaf.who.title: Who is the SIELE for?
testdaf.who.text: The SIELE (Servicio Internacional de Evaluación de la Lengua Española) is taken on a computer at an exam centre. It comes from the Instituto Cervantes, UNAM in Mexico, the Universidad de Salamanca and the Universidad de Buenos Aires. People take it for study and work when the institution accepts it. It doesn't count for Spanish nationality, according to the SIELE site. That route needs the DELE at A2 or above, plus the CCSE.

lid.who.title: Who is the CCSE for?
lid.who.badge.noCefr: No CEFR level — a knowledge test
lid.who.text: The CCSE does not test your level of Spanish but your knowledge of Spain's constitution, institutions, society and culture. Most people applying for Spanish nationality by residence need it, usually together with a DELE A2 or higher, and some applicants are exempt. grammatik.artikel.intro: Spanish has four words for “the”: el, la, los, las. It has four for “a” or “some”: un, una, unos, unas. The article shows if the noun is masculine or feminine, singular or plural.
grammatik.ja-nein-fragen.intro: A yes/no question can use the same words as a statement. Only ¿…? in writing and your voice going up show that it is a question. Put no before the verb to say “not”.
grammatik.w-fragen.intro: Question words always have a written accent: qué, quién, dónde, adónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, por qué. A written question opens with ¿ and closes with ?.
grammatik.praesens.intro: Spanish verbs end in -ar, -er or -ir. Take off the ending and add the one for the person: hablar → hablo, hablas, habla. Use the present for now, for habits and for facts.
grammatik.verb-position-2.intro: Spanish has two verbs for “to be”. Use ser for who or what something is. Use estar for where something is and how it is right now: Soy Ana. Estoy en casa. Estoy cansada.
grammatik.konjugation.intro: The most useful Spanish verbs do not follow the rules: ser, estar, ir, tener, hacer, venir. Some are irregular only in the yo form: salgo, pongo, conozco.
grammatik.plural.intro: One house, two houses: after a vowel add -s (casa → casas). After a consonant add -es (ciudad → ciudades). The article and the adjective become plural too: las casas blancas.
grammatik.possessivartikel.intro: Whose is it? Mi casa, tu coche, su hijo. The possessive matches the thing you have, not the person who has it: mis llaves, nuestra casa. Owners can also come with de: el coche de Ana.
grammatik.imperativ.intro: Spanish has four forms: tú (habla), usted (hable), vosotros (hablad), ustedes (hablen). Negative forms use the subjunctive: no hables, no hable, no habléis, no hablen. Pronouns go on the end of an affirmative form and before a negative one: dímelo, no me lo digas.
grammatik.aduso.intro: Use y (and), o (or), pero (but) and porque (because) to join words and sentences. Before an i- sound, y becomes e. Before an o- sound, o becomes u. Use también and tampoco to say “also” and “not either”.
grammatik.nomen.intro: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, even a table or a street. Most nouns ending in -o are masculine (el libro) and most ending in -a are feminine (la casa). Learn each noun with its article.
grammatik.komposita.intro: To say what is happening right now, use estar + gerund: Estoy trabajando. Están comiendo. -ar verbs take -ando, -er and -ir verbs take -iendo. Spanish uses this form less than English: for habits and for plans, use the normal present.
grammatik.wortarten.intro: Each word does a job in the sentence. Knowing the job helps you use the word: a noun has a gender, a verb changes for the person, an adjective matches its noun.
grammatik.akkusativ.intro: The direct object is the person or thing the verb acts on. Pronouns: me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las. They go before the conjugated verb: Veo a Ana. La veo. A person takes the personal a: Veo a Ana. A thing doesn't: Veo la casa.
grammatik.dativ.intro: Indirect object pronouns say who gets something: me, te, le, nos, os, les. Le doy el libro a Ana. When le or les meets lo, la, los or las, it becomes se: Se lo doy.
grammatik.modalverben.intro: To say what you must, can or want to do, use a conjugated verb + an infinitive: Tengo que trabajar. Puedo ayudar. Quiero descansar. Hay que pedir cita. The second verb never changes.
grammatik.negation.intro: Put no before the verb: No trabajo. Spanish uses double negatives: No veo a nadie. No como nunca carne. If the negative word comes before the verb, drop no: Nadie viene. Nunca como carne.
grammatik.perfekt.intro: In Spain, use the pretérito perfecto for things that happened today, this week or this year, and for your life so far: Hoy he trabajado mucho. It is haber + a participle: he hablado, has comido, ha vivido.
grammatik.satzstellung.intro: muy goes before an adjective or adverb: muy cansado. mucho goes with a verb: Trabajo mucho. With a noun, mucho agrees: mucha gente, muchos problemas. poco, bastante and demasiado follow the same pattern.
grammatik.wechselpraepositionen.intro: Use a for movement towards a place: Voy a Madrid. Use en for being in a place: Estoy en Madrid. With de… a and desde… hasta you say where a journey or a time starts and ends.
grammatik.positionsverben.intro: These verbs work like gustar: the thing or activity is the subject, and the person takes me, te, le, nos, os, les. Me encanta este barrio. Me encantan los lunes. The verb agrees with the thing, not with the person.
grammatik.praepositionen.intro: Many Spanish verbs take one fixed preposition: pensar en, soñar con, depender de, acordarse de, tardar en. It often isn't the one English uses, so learn the verb and the preposition together.
grammatik.trennbare-verben.intro: To talk about plans and the near future, use ir + a + infinitive: Voy a llamar al médico. Mañana vamos a buscar piso. Only ir changes. The second verb stays in the infinitive.
grammatik.zusammengesetzte-verben.intro: Use the pretérito indefinido for finished events at a finished time: Ayer fui al médico. Llegué a España en 2022. Regular endings: -é, -aste, -ó for -ar verbs; -í, -iste, -ió for -er and -ir verbs. Many common verbs are irregular: fui, tuve, hice, estuve, dije.
grammatik.als-oder-wenn.intro: Both can mean for, but they look in different directions. Para looks ahead: a goal, a person who receives something, a destination, a deadline. Por looks at the cause or the way: why it happens, where it passes, how, at what price.
grammatik.n-deklination.intro: Use the imperfecto to talk about how things used to be: habits and descriptions in the past. Antes vivía en Rabat. La casa era pequeña. -ar verbs take -aba, -er and -ir verbs take -ía. Only three verbs are irregular: ser, ir and ver.
grammatik.genitiv.intro: To avoid repeating a noun, use a possessive pronoun: Mi casa es pequeña. ¿Y la tuya? It agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. After ser, you normally drop the article: Este abrigo es mío.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination.intro: Most adjectives go after the noun: un coche rojo. A few can go before it and lose their ending before a masculine singular noun: buen, mal, primer, tercer, algún, ningún. Gran is short before any singular noun. Some adjectives change meaning with position: un gran hombre, un hombre grande.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination-a2.intro: Add -mente to the feminine form of an adjective to make an adverb: rápida → rápidamente, fácil → fácilmente. Adverbs describe a verb: Hablas bien. Adjectives describe a noun: Es un buen médico.
grammatik.ordinalzahlen.intro: Ordinals up to ten are worth knowing: primero, segundo, tercero… They agree with the noun: la segunda calle. Before a masculine noun: primer, tercer. Dates use normal numbers: el 3 de mayo. Addresses and floors use ordinals: segundo B.
grammatik.zahlen.intro: From 0 to 1000. Up to 30 most numbers are one word: dieciséis, veintidós. After that, use y: treinta y uno. Uno shortens before a noun: un euro, veintiún años, and it agrees with feminine nouns: una casa.
grammatik.adjektive-nach-sein.intro: An adjective matches its noun in gender and number, and it usually comes after the noun: una casa blanca, los coches nuevos.
grammatik.gern.intro: In Spanish, the thing you like is the subject: me gusta el café (coffee pleases me). One thing or an action: me gusta. More than one thing: me gustan.
grammatik.praeteritum-sein-haben.intro: Some verbs change a vowel in the stem when it is stressed: querer → quiero, poder → puedo, pedir → pido, jugar → juego. The endings stay regular, and nosotros and vosotros do not change.
grammatik.berufe-mit-in.intro: Use hay to say that something exists: Hay una farmacia aquí. Use está or están to say where a known thing is: La farmacia está en la plaza.
grammatik.konjunktiv2-hoeflich.intro: In Spanish, you are polite with a question and the right verb form: ¿Puede ayudarme? ¿Me pone un café? To ask for something at an office or shop, use quería or me gustaría: Quería pedir cita.
grammatik.infinitiv-mit-zu.intro: The present subjunctive swaps the vowel: -ar verbs take -e endings (hable), -er and -ir verbs take -a endings (coma, viva). Most irregular forms come from the yo form of the present: tengo → tenga, hago → haga. You will usually see it after que: Quiero que vengas.
grammatik.praeteritum-plusquamperfekt.in: In a story, the indefinido tells what happened: Llegué a Madrid. Sonó el teléfono. The imperfecto describes the background and habits: Hacía frío. Vivía en un piso pequeño. A background action can be interrupted by an event: Dormía cuando sonó el teléfono.
grammatik.indirekte-fragen.intro: To report in the present, use dice que for statements and pregunta si for yes/no questions. Question words stay and keep their accent: No sé dónde está. ¿Sabes cuándo abren? The word order is simple, and there are no ¿? around the indirect part.
grammatik.passiv.intro: In everyday Spanish, se is the normal way to leave out who does something: Se alquila piso. Se venden pisos. Se vive bien aquí. The passive with ser + participle (El puente fue construido en 1920) belongs mostly to news and formal writing.
grammatik.passiv-b1.intro: Use the pluscuamperfecto for something that had already happened before another moment in the past: Cuando llegué, el tren ya había salido. It is había + a participle: había comido, habías llegado, habían salido.
grammatik.wortbildung-nomen.intro: The ending of a Spanish noun often tells you what it means and its gender. -ción and -dad make feminine nouns: la información, la ciudad. -miento makes masculine ones: el nacimiento. -ero/-era is a person with a job, and -ería is the shop. -ito and -illo make things small.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen-b1.in: If something started in the past and is still going on, Spanish uses the present tense: Vivo aquí desde 2020 (a starting point). Vivo aquí desde hace tres años (a period). You can also say Hace tres años que vivo aquí, or Llevo tres años aquí.
grammatik.infinitiv-ohne-zu.intro: Ask who does the second action. The same person: use the infinitive (Quiero ir). A different person: use que + subjunctive (Quiero que vayas). Don't say Quiero que yo vaya.
grammatik.funktionen-von-werden.intro: Use the condicional for polite wishes and requests, advice, and what you would do: Me gustaría pedir cita. ¿Podría ayudarme? Yo que tú, hablaría con el casero. Add -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían to the infinitive.
grammatik.konjunktiv2.intro: Use the imperfect subjunctive when a past or conditional verb asks for the subjunctive: Quería que vinieras. Me gustaría que vinieras. Use it with ojalá for a wish that is unlikely now: Ojalá tuviera más tiempo. To make it, take the ellos form of the indefinido, drop -ron and add -ra or -se.
grammatik.relativpronomen.intro: A relative clause adds information about a noun. Use que for people and things: la chica que trabaja conmigo, el piso que quiero. Use donde for places: el barrio donde vivo. Use lo que when there is no noun: No entiendo lo que dice.
grammatik.irgend.intro: Use se + me, te, le… + verb when something happens to you by accident: Se me olvidó la llave. Se le ha roto el móvil. Se nos acabó el café. The verb agrees with the thing, not with the person.
grammatik.fokuspartikeln.intro: Spanish has no single verb for “become”. Use ponerse for a quick change of mood or health, volverse for a change of character, hacerse for a profession or belief, quedarse for the state after an event, and convertirse en + noun for a big change.
grammatik.negationswoerter.intro: Spanish uses the future for a guess about now: Serán las tres. The future perfect is a guess about something that has just happened: Habrá salido. The conditional is a guess about the past: Estaría cansado.
grammatik.nomen-verb-verbindungen.intro: Some verbs and nouns go together, and another verb sounds wrong: tomar una decisión, hacer caso, dar un paseo, pedir cita, echar de menos. English often suggests the wrong verb, so learn the pair as one phrase.
grammatik.partizip-als-adjektiv.intro: Use estar + a participle for the state something is in after an action: La tienda está cerrada. La carta está escrita. The participle agrees like an adjective: cerrado, cerrada, cerrados, cerradas.
grammatik.adjektive-als-nomen.intro: Lo + adjective talks about an idea, not a thing or a person: lo bueno (the good thing), lo importante (what matters). The adjective doesn't change. Lo que means what, the thing that: Lo que necesito es tiempo.
grammatik.zweiteilige-konnektoren.intro: An opinion you state takes the indicative: Creo que viene. A denied opinion, a doubt or a possibility takes the subjunctive: No creo que venga. Dudo que venga. Es posible que venga. A fact you confirm takes the indicative: Es verdad que viene.
grammatik.konditionalsaetze.intro: For a real, possible condition, use si + present. The result can be present, future or an imperative: Si llueve, me quedo en casa. Si tienes tiempo, llámame. In a real condition, never use the future or the present subjunctive after si.
grammatik.konsekutivsaetze.intro: aunque takes the indicative for a fact you state and the subjunctive when something is unknown or doesn't matter to you: Aunque tenía fiebre, fui a trabajar. Aunque llueva, saldré. A consequence: tan cansado que…, tanto trabajo que…, de modo que…
grammatik.zumal-wohingegen.intro: When you report with a past verb (dijo que…), the verb usually moves one step back: vivo → vivía, he llamado → había llamado, vendré → vendría. Orders and wishes take the imperfect subjunctive: ¡Ven! → Me pidió que fuera.
grammatik.modalsaetze.intro: For something unreal or unlikely now, use si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional: Si tuviera dinero, compraría un piso. For a past that didn't happen, use si + hubiera + participle, then habría + participle: Si hubiera sabido, habría venido.
grammatik.reflexive-verben.intro: Many daily-routine verbs need a small pronoun that matches the person: me levanto, te duchas, se viste. In the dictionary the verb ends in -se: levantarse. The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb.
grammatik.nebensaetze-weil-dass.intro: Give a reason with porque (after the main idea) or como (at the start). Give a result with así que or por eso. To say what you think or what someone says, use que: Creo que está cerrado. Dice que viene mañana.
grammatik.komparativ-superlativ.intro: To compare, use más… que, menos… que or tan… como: Este piso es más caro que el otro. To say “the most”, use el, la, los or las + más: Es el más barato. Four words have their own forms: mejor, peor, mayor, menor.
grammatik.lokale-praepositionen.intro: To say where something is, use estar + a place word: Las llaves están encima de la mesa. Most place words end in de: al lado de, delante de, debajo de. Aquí, ahí and allí say how far away it is from you.
grammatik.positionsadverbien.intro: Say how often with siempre, a menudo, a veces, casi nunca and nunca. Use soler + infinitive for what you usually do: Suelo comer a las dos. Solemos ir andando.
grammatik.personalpronomen.intro: Yo, tú, él, ella, usted, nosotros, vosotros, ellos, ellas, ustedes. The verb ending already shows the person, so Spanish often drops the pronoun: Vivo en Madrid.
grammatik.indefinitpronomen.intro: algo is something, nada is nothing. alguien is someone, nadie is no one. algún and ningún go with a noun: ¿Hay algún problema? No hay ningún problema. otro means another: otro café.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen.intro: ¿Qué hora es? Es la una. Son las ocho. At what time? A las ocho. Use el lunes for “on Monday”, los lunes for “on Mondays”, and por la mañana for “in the morning”.
grammatik.futur.intro: Use the futuro simple for predictions, promises and plans: Mañana lloverá. Te llamaré esta noche. Add the endings -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án to the whole infinitive. A few common verbs have a short stem: tendré, podré, haré.
grammatik.temporale-nebensaetze.intro: With cuando, en cuanto and hasta que, use the indicative for habits and the past: Cuando llego, ceno. Cuando llegué, cené. For the future, use the subjunctive: Cuando llegue, cenaré. Never use the future after cuando.
grammatik.da-wo-woerter.intro: After a preposition, Spanish uses mí and ti, not yo and tú: para mí, sin ti. The other persons stay the same: con él, para ella, sin nosotros. With con there are two special forms: conmigo and contigo.
grammatik.lassen.intro: A helper verb + an infinitive or gerund adds a meaning of time: Acabo de comer (a moment ago). Vuelvo a llamar (again). Dejo de fumar (stop). Sigo trabajando (still). Llevo dos años viviendo aquí (for two years so far). Learn each one with its little word.
grammatik.modalpartikeln.intro: Small words like pues, bueno, o sea, es que, vamos, venga and vale keep a conversation going: they react, hesitate, explain, rephrase or close. They belong to speech and informal messages, not to a formal email.
grammatik.adjektive-mit-praepositionen.i: Many adjectives take a fixed preposition: harto de, capaz de, contento con, interesado en, preocupado por, acostumbrado a. Add a noun, an infinitive for the same person, or que + subjunctive for another person.
grammatik.konnektoren-grund-gegengrund.i: Linkers show how two ideas connect. aunque = although: Aunque estoy cansado, voy a trabajar. sin embargo = however, además = also, en cambio = on the other hand, por lo tanto = so, therefore. Use a comma after sin embargo, además and por lo tanto.
grammatik.finalsaetze.intro: To say why you do something, use para. If one person does both actions, use para + infinitive: Estudio para aprobar. If the second action is someone else's, use para que + subjunctive: Te llamo para que lo sepas.
grammatik.zustandspassiv.intro: In Spain the question is whether the time is over. A time that still includes now takes the perfecto: Hoy he ido al banco. A finished time takes the indefinido: Ayer fui al banco. Life experience with no date also takes the perfecto: ¿Has estado en Sevilla?
grammatik.relativsaetze-was-wo.intro: Use the indicative for something you know exists, and the subjunctive for something unknown or that doesn't exist: Conozco a alguien que sabe inglés. Busco a alguien que sepa inglés. A preposition goes first: el piso en el que vivo, la persona con quien hablé.
grammatik.konjunktiv-1.intro: The main verb chooses the subjunctive tense. Present main verb: quiero que vengas, espero que hayas llegado. Past main verb: quería que vinieras, me alegré de que hubieras venido. The pluperfect subjunctive, hubiera hecho, looks further back.
grammatik.subjektive-modalverben.intro: Small words change the meaning. Deber + infinitive says what is right: Debes pedir cita. Deber de guesses: Debe de tener cuarenta años. Haber de is formal obligation, venir a means roughly, and llegar a means going as far as: Llegó a ser directora.
grammatik.passiversatz.intro: Spanish has other ways to set a condition. De + infinitive is compact: De haberlo sabido, no habría venido. Como + subjunctive warns: Como no pagues, te cortan la luz. A no ser que means unless, and siempre que and con tal de que mean as long as: all three take the subjunctive.
grammatik.partizipialattribute.intro: Formal Spanish has three more relatives. El cual follows a preposition or comma: el motivo por el cual. Lo cual refers to a whole idea: No ha pagado, lo cual es grave. Cuyo means whose and agrees with what follows it: la vecina cuyos hijos…
grammatik.nominalisierung.intro: Formal Spanish often turns a verb or adjective into a noun: subir → la subida, escaso → la escasez. A noun phrase such as la subida de los precios says in few words what a full clause says. Everyday speech keeps the verbs.
grammatik.nominale-praepositionen.intro: Letters, reports and contracts link ideas with formal words. Debido a and a raíz de give a cause, en virtud de gives a legal basis, no obstante marks a contrast, and por consiguiente a result. Check what comes next: a noun, a clause or a new sentence.
grammatik.irreale-vergleiche.intro: Como si compares something with a situation that isn't real. Same time: imperfect subjunctive, Habla como si lo supiera todo. Earlier: pluperfect subjunctive, Me miró como si no me hubiera visto nunca. Ni que rejects an exaggeration: ¡Ni que fuera rico!
grammatik.futur-2.intro: A clause without a conjugated verb says the same thing in fewer words. Al + infinitive: Al llegar, vi la carta. The gerund: Viendo que no venía, lo llamé. The participle: Terminada la reunión, nos fuimos.
grammatik.es-korrelat.intro: A cleft sentence puts the spotlight on one part of the message. Use ser + the part in focus + a relative word: Fue Ana quien llamó. Es aquí donde vivo. Or start with what you want to explain: Lo que necesito es tiempo.
grammatik.textkohaerenz.intro: A good text holds together. Reference words point back: este, dicho, ello. Neuter lo stands for a quality: ¿Es médica? Sí, lo es. Ellipsis leaves out what is clear: Ella vive en Madrid y él, en Sevilla. Register decides which of them you use.
grammatik.verbpraefixe.intro: A prefix changes a word's meaning. Des- undoes it: deshacer. Re- repeats it: reabrir. Pre- comes before: prever. In- denies: inútil. Sobre- goes over: sobrecargar. Contra- opposes: contradecir. A verb with a prefix usually conjugates like its base verb: deshice, prevén.
grammatik.nutzen-benutzen.intro: Some adjectives change meaning with ser and estar: Es listo (clever), Está listo (ready). Es aburrido (boring), Está aburrido (bored). Events take ser for their place and time: La fiesta es en mi casa. People and things take estar: Mi casa está en el centro.
grammatik.verben-als-nomen.intro: After a wish or a feeling about someone else, use que + subjunctive: Quiero que vengas. Me alegra que estés mejor. Ojalá also takes the subjunctive: Ojalá haga sol. For facts and opinions, use the indicative: Creo que viene.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.intro: Spanish uses el, la, los, las for things in general with gustar: Me gusta el café. With tener, comprar and beber, the plain noun is normal: Tengo coche. Bebo agua. No article for jobs and languages: Es médica. Hablo español.
grammatik.welcher-dieser.intro: This one, that one, that one over there: este is near you, ese is near the other person, aquel is far from you both. They match the noun: esta casa, esos libros. Esto and eso name something unknown.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.brief:
Why “Me gusta el café” but “Bebo café”? Why “Es médica” with no article?

  • —No article: jobs, languages, tener or beber + a general thing.
  • un, unaOne of many, or a new thing: hay una farmacia.
  • el, laThe one we both know, things in general with gustar, days of the week.
kultur.duzen-siezen.cardIntro: English has only one word for you.
kultur.pfand.cardIntro: In the UK, people queue for buses, shops and many other things.
kultur.sonntagsruhe.cardIntro: On Sundays, many shops in the UK open for fewer hours.
kultur.trinkgeld.cardIntro: In a UK restaurant, a tip of about 10 to 12.5% is normal.
kultur.bundeslaender.cardIntro: The UK is made up of four nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
kultur.feiertage.cardIntro: A bank holiday is a public holiday: many people do not work, and banks and offices close.
kultur.muelltrennung.cardIntro: In the UK, your local council collects rubbish and recycling from your home.
kultur.termine.cardIntro: In the UK, you usually book an appointment before you see a doctor, a dentist or a hairdresser.
kultur.anmeldung.cardIntro: There is no residence registration in the UK, so you do not have to report your address to the city.
kultur.krankenversicherung.cardIntro: The NHS (National Health Service) gives most health care free at the point of use.
kultur.mieten.cardIntro: When you rent a flat in the UK, the monthly rent is only part of the cost.
kultur.schulsystem.cardIntro: In England children go to primary school and then secondary school, and they stay in education or training until they are 18.
kultur.ausbildung.cardIntro: After school, young people in the UK can either go to university or train in a job as an apprentice.
kultur.kuendigung.cardIntro: When you leave a job in the UK, or an employer ends your contract, a period of notice usually applies.
The BBC is the UK's public broadcaster, and it is paid for mainly by a licence fee rather than by adverts.
kultur.vereine.cardIntro: Much of social life in the UK happens in clubs, societies and volunteering groups, which are usually informal and easy to join.
kultur.foederalismus.cardIntro: Ask who runs education in the UK and the honest answer is: it depends where you are.
kultur.sozialversicherung.cardIntro: National Insurance sounds like an insurance scheme, but in practice it works largely as a tax that also builds your entitlement to certain benefits.
kultur.wahlen.cardIntro: In a UK general election you cast a single vote for one candidate in your local constituency, and you do not vote for the Prime Minister at all.

tdf.start.intro: The SIELE has no pass mark: each test gets a score from 0 to 250 and a CEFR level, and each institution decides what it asks for.
tdf.sourcing: This set is built like the reading and writing part of the SIELE (the S2 modality), but it is shorter and it isn't the real exam. The real Reading test has 5 tasks, 38 questions and 60 minutes; this set has 3 tasks and 20 questions, at about B1, B2 and C1. The first one follows a real task type (three texts, statements to match). The other two are plain multiple-choice reading for practice: the real B2 and C1 reading tasks are gap texts, and you can practise those in the SIELE sets by level. The real Writing test has 2 tasks and 50 minutes; here you do the longer one, an opinion text. All texts and questions were written by icanspeak Spanish. Nothing is copied from a SIELE paper or demo exam. For an official demo, see siele.org.
tdf.scoringNote: The SIELE has no pass mark. Each of its four tests gets a score from 0 to 250, and the score is matched to a CEFR level. The rating below isn't a SIELE score and doesn't give you a level. It's only rough feedback on this practice set. The institution you are applying to tells you what you need.

Two kinds of topic sit side by side here, and each one says which kind it is:
“From class” – from a real class discussion.
“Facts” – publicly checkable facts about rules, institutions and procedures in Spain (laws, amounts, who is responsible). Written by icanspeak Spanish, not taken from a lesson.
What is deliberately NOT here: claims about “the Spanish character”. Nothing is claimed about people – only about rules, figures and responsibilities, and where practice differs between comunidades autónomas, places or people, the topic says so.
Amounts and deadlines change. Every figure carries a date; if in doubt, the official source is right, not this page. This is general orientation, not legal advice.

sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.1: Full sentences, not a list: “Tengo 29 años.”, not just “29”. Age goes with tener, and a job takes no article: “Soy electricista.”
sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.2: End with your free time: it is a natural next question.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.0: “En la foto veo …” is the easiest way to start. People take a: veo a una mujer. Things don't: veo un tren.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.1: “Creo que …” and “a lo mejor …” let you guess without being sure.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.2: The last sentence is about you: that is a natural next question.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.0: First count (“dos personas”), then say the place, then the action. This order always works.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.1: For what is happening now, use estar + -ando or -iendo: está cocinando, está comiendo.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.0: Fruta and verdura are usually singular in Spanish: compro fruta. But manzanas and plátanos are plural.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.1: “en la caja”, “con tarjeta”, “en efectivo”: learn the little word with the phrase.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.2: A time phrase at the end (“los sábados”, “una vez a la semana”) sounds practised straight away.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.0: Two people, two descriptions: first the boy, then the girl.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.1: One sentence about the weather, with hacer: hace buen tiempo, hace sol, hace calor.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.2: “porque” joins your reason to your sentence: me gusta el parque porque es tranquilo.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-nachbarschaftsfes: Say what is en primer plano and al fondo: that is the step from A1 to A2.
A guess with a reason: “Creo que es …, porque …”
End with a comparison with your own life or country. At A2 a comparison like this is a natural last step.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.0: Say how someone feels and why: “Parece preocupada. A lo mejor …” Pictures with people often invite this question.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.1: Say what you can and can't see: “Solo vemos su brazo.”
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.2: A real detail from your own life (“a veces espero una semana”) is worth more than a general sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-bewerbungsgesprae: Use place words to organise what you say: a la izquierda, a la derecha, enfrente de, al fondo.
Show that a guess is a guess (“Diría que …”, “puede que esté …”) and give a reason.
The part in the past is expected at B1: the indefinido for the event (“hice”), the imperfecto for how you felt (“estaba”).
One sentence with “En mi opinión”: giving your opinion is the real B1 part.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.0: “Supongo que …, porque …” joins a guess and a reason in one sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.1: Explain a word (FP) instead of just saying it.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.2: The “¿por qué?” question gets a real answer with “porque” or “Una razón podría ser que …”.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.0: Show how you know something: “Se nota que …, porque …”
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.1: Give a real example from your own life instead of a general complaint.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.2: “Ahora …” shows how things have changed, which is a useful B1 skill.
You react to the other person instead of working through your own list.
Disagree politely at least once: that is what the task tests.
At the end you clearly agree on every point.
Polite forms with the conditional: propondría, elegiría, ¿podríamos …?
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.0: The description is short. At B2 it is the way in, not the task.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.1: Both sides are there, with the linking words for them: una ventaja clara, por otro lado, no hay que olvidar.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.2: Saying “no es solo …, también …” shows you have really thought the question through.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.3: The personal ending is honest rather than perfect: that is harder to say and sounds more mature.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.0: Something you notice in the picture supports your argument (“Lo que me llama la atención es que …”), not just general knowledge.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.1: The objection to your own view is there (“Algunos dirán que …”) and you answer it.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.2: The difference between “días de oficina para todo el equipo” and “una regla para cada persona” is a fine distinction. That is exactly what separates B2 from B1.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-baustelle-innenst: A detail from the picture (the flats right next to the site) becomes part of the argument, not just a description.
“La verdadera cuestión no es si …, sino cómo …” moves the discussion on: a strong B2 phrase.
The opinion ends with conditions, not a simple yes or no. That is more balanced and easier to defend.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.0: A system is explained, not just judged.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.1: The counter-argument and your answer to it are both there.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.2: “Reciclar limita el daño; no resuelve el problema”: a short, sharp sentence at the end stays with the listener.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.3: The comparison with your own country doesn't judge; it describes a difference.

nsw.why.title: Why look things up?
nsw.why.p1: Nobody learns every form by heart – native speakers look things up too. If you know where the answer is, you write with more confidence and don't have to guess.
nsw.why.p2: And the best part: every time you look something up, it sticks a little better. You learn along the way.

nsw.tip2.p: A word like “fui” or “roto”? The verb tables give you the base form.
nsw.tip3.p: Irregular verbs and verbs with prepositions come up in many exams. Going through the lists once is worth it.
nsw.tip4.p: Every page can be printed, shared and played as a live quiz with the whole class.

sprachen.title: English around the world
sprachen.lead: Where English is spoken, which languages it is related to – and how close your first language is to English.
sprachen.stat.native: people speak English as their first language
sprachen.stat.second: speak it as a second or foreign language
sprachen.stat.official: countries with English as an official language
sprachen.stat.eu: the language with the most speakers in the world
sprachen.map.title: Where English is spoken
sprachen.map.lead: Tap a country or a dot. The colours show how English is used there.
sprachen.map.empty: Pick a country on the map – or in the list below.
sprachen.count.native: people have English as their first language
sprachen.count.minority: people speak only English at home
sprachen.count.dialect: people can hold a conversation in English
sprachen.count.note: Rounded figures from censuses: USA 2022, Australia 2021, India 2011.
sprachen.c.GBR: About 69 million people live in the UK, and almost all of them speak English. Welsh is also an official language in Wales, and Scottish Gaelic, Scots, Irish, Ulster Scots and Cornish are protected minority languages.
sprachen.c.IRL: Irish (Gaelic) is the national and first official language; English is the second official language. In everyday life almost everybody speaks English, and Irish English has its own words, like grand (fine) and craic (fun).
sprachen.c.USA: More people speak English as their first language here than in any other country. About three in four people speak only English at home; Spanish is the second most common language. Congress never passed a law on an official language, but a presidential order in 2025 named English.
sprachen.c.CAN: Canada has two official languages, English and French. English is the first language of more than half of Canadians; French is the main language in Quebec. Canadian spelling mixes British and American: colour, but tire.
sprachen.c.AUS: No law names an official language, but English is the national language. About 72% of people speak only English at home (2021 census). Australians like to shorten words: arvo (afternoon), brekkie (breakfast).
sprachen.c.NZL: New Zealand has three official languages: English, Māori and New Zealand Sign Language. English was used everywhere long before a law made it official in 2026. Many Māori words are part of everyday English here, like kia ora (hello).
sprachen.c.IND: English is an official language of India’s central government, next to Hindi. In the 2011 census about 129 million people said they speak English – very few as their first language. Indian English has its own words, like prepone (to move something to an earlier time).
sprachen.c.PAK: Urdu is the national language. Urdu and English are both official, and English is used in government, the courts, universities and much of business.
sprachen.c.PHL: Filipino and English are the official languages. English is used in schools, government and business, and many people mix the two in everyday talk – often called Taglish.
sprachen.c.SGP: Singapore has four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin Chinese and Tamil. English is the language of work and school, and in the 2020 census it was the language most families used at home. Singlish, the local everyday English, adds words like lah.
sprachen.c.HKG: A British colony until 1997. Chinese and English are both official. Most people speak Cantonese, and a little over half of the population also speaks English.
sprachen.c.MLT: Maltese and English are the official languages, and laws are written in both. Almost nine in ten people say they can hold a conversation in English, and many students come here to learn it.
sprachen.c.NGA: Nigeria has more than 500 languages. English is the official language of government and schools, and Nigerian Pidgin, an English-based language, connects people all over the country.
sprachen.c.GHA: English is the official language, used in government and schools. Ghana has dozens of local languages; Akan (Twi) is the most widely spoken.
sprachen.c.SLE: English is the official language. In everyday life many people use Krio, an English-based creole, to talk across language groups.
sprachen.c.LBR: From 1822, freed and free-born African Americans settled here, and their English became the language of the state. Today English is the official language, and more than 20 local languages are spoken too.
sprachen.c.CMR: Cameroon has two official languages, French and English. English is mainly used in the Northwest and Southwest regions, where many people also speak Cameroonian Pidgin English.
sprachen.c.KEN: Swahili and English are the official languages; Swahili is also the national language. English is used in schools, the courts and business, while Swahili is spoken more widely in everyday life.
sprachen.c.UGA: English is the official language, used in schools, business and the courts. Swahili became the second official language in 2005, and Luganda is widely spoken around Kampala.
sprachen.c.TZA: Swahili is the main language of the country. English is used next to it as a working language, for example in secondary schools, universities and business.
sprachen.c.RWA: Rwanda has four official languages: Kinyarwanda, English, French and Swahili. Almost everyone speaks Kinyarwanda. In 2008 the government made English the language of schools and of government work instead of French.
sprachen.c.ZMB: English is the official language, used in government and schools. Bemba and Nyanja are widely spoken local languages.
sprachen.c.ZWE: Since its 2013 constitution, Zimbabwe has 16 official languages, including English. Shona and Ndebele are the most widely spoken; English is the main language of government, business and schools.
sprachen.c.BWA: English is the official language. Setswana is the national language, and most people speak it at home.
sprachen.c.NAM: When Namibia became independent in 1990, it chose English as its only official language, although few people spoke it at home. Oshiwambo is the most common home language; Afrikaans and German are spoken too.
sprachen.c.ZAF: South Africa has twelve official languages, including South African Sign Language. English is the home language of fewer than one in ten people, but it is a main language of business, politics and the media.
sprachen.c.PNG: Papua New Guinea has more than 800 languages – more than any other country. English is an official language, used in government, the courts and schools; Tok Pisin, an English-based creole, is the everyday common language.
sprachen.c.FJI: English, Fijian (iTaukei) and Fiji Hindi are the main languages. English was the only official language until 1997 and is still the common language of government, business and education.
sprachen.c.JAM: English is the official language, used in schools, government and the news. In everyday life most people speak Jamaican Patois (Patwa), an English-based creole with many words from African languages.
sprachen.c.TTO: English is the official language. In everyday life people speak Trinidadian or Tobagonian Creole, which are based on English.
sprachen.c.BHS: English is the official language. Many Bahamians also speak Bahamian Creole, which is based on English.
sprachen.c.BRB: English is the official language. Bajan, the local English-based creole, is spoken in everyday life.
sprachen.c.GUY: Guyana is the only country in mainland South America with English as its official language. Most people grow up speaking Guyanese Creole (Creolese), which is based on English.
sprachen.c.BLZ: Belize is the only country in Central America with English as its official language. Belizean Kriol, Spanish and Mayan languages are widely spoken too.
sprachen.c.NLD: English is not official, but about nine in ten Dutch people can hold a conversation in it. Children learn it at school, and many university courses are taught in English.
sprachen.c.DNK: English is not official, but most Danes speak it well. Children start English early at school, and films and series from abroad are usually subtitled, not dubbed.
sprachen.c.SWE: English is not official, but most Swedes speak it well – it is taught from primary school, and English films and series are subtitled, not dubbed.
sprachen.c.MYS: Malay is the official and national language. English was official too until 1967 and is still widely used in business, higher education and the cities.
sprachen.m.gibraltar: A British Overseas Territory at the southern tip of Spain. English is the official language; most Gibraltarians also speak Spanish and Llanito, a local mix of Andalusian Spanish and English.
sprachen.m.bermuda: A British Overseas Territory in the North Atlantic. English is the official language; some families also speak Portuguese – their families came from the Azores.
sprachen.m.falklands: A British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, with about 3,700 people (2021 census). English is the official language.
sprachen.benrath.text: In Europe, English is the main language of the UK and Ireland, and an official language in Malta and Gibraltar. In the Netherlands and Scandinavia it is not official, but most people speak it well.
sprachen.tree.title: The language family
sprachen.tree.lead: English is a Germanic language and belongs to the large Indo-European family. Many languages from Iceland to India share the same roots.
sprachen.tree.otherLead: These languages are not related to English. That doesn't make English harder – it just means you learn words fresh instead of recognising them.
sprachen.tree.names: Language names are given in English.
sprachen.cmp.title: How close is your language?
sprachen.cmp.lead: Pick your first language. Eight basic words show how much you already bring with you.
sprachen.cmp.fehler: Typical mistakes with this first language
sprachen.cmp.persisch: Surprise: Persian is related to English! Both are Indo-European. Compare barādar – brother, mādar – mother, nām – name.
sprachen.cmp.russisch: Russian is Slavic – another branch of the same family: брат – brother, три – three, вода – water. Russian nouns have six cases; English nouns have none, and only pronouns change (I – me, she – her).
sprachen.cmp.ukrainisch: Ukrainian is Slavic and distantly related to English: брат – brother, ніч – night, вода – water. Ukrainian nouns have seven cases; in English, word order does that job.
sprachen.cmp.polnisch: Polish is Slavic: brat – brother, noc – night, woda – water. Polish nouns have seven cases; in English, word order does that job – Ola sees Tom is not the same as Tom sees Ola.
sprachen.cmp.franzoesisch: French is Romance, English is Germanic – both Indo-European. But after the Norman Conquest of 1066, English took thousands of words from French: table, beef, people, government. So you will recognise a lot.
sprachen.cmp.italienisch: Italian comes from Latin – and so do many English words, often through French: nation, family, important, possible. The short everyday words are mostly Germanic, though.
sprachen.cmp.spanisch: Spanish is Romance and distantly related to English: noche – night, tres – three. Many longer English words come from Latin, so they look familiar: hospital, animal, possible. Hermano and brother, though, have different roots.
sprachen.cmp.arabisch: Arabic belongs to the Afro-Asiatic family and is not related to English. But English has many words from Arabic, often through other languages: sugar (sukkar), coffee (qahwa), algebra (al-jabr), zero (ṣifr).
sprachen.cmp.tuerkisch: Turkish is a Turkic language and not related to English. Still, there are bridges: yoghurt and kiosk came into English through Turkish – and Turkish has taken words like futbol from English.
sprachen.cmp.chinesisch: Chinese is Sino-Tibetan and not related to English. Good news: English has no tones, and verbs hardly change – only the -s in she works. And the word tea came from the Hokkien Chinese word tê, through Dutch traders.
sprachen.cmp.vietnamesisch: Vietnamese is Austroasiatic and not related to English. But you already know the Latin alphabet – that makes reading and writing easier. And English has no tones.
sprachen.cmp.tagalog: Tagalog is Austronesian and not related to English – ina, gabi and bahay have completely different roots. But English is an official language in the Philippines, and Filipino has taken many English words.
sprachen.cmp.deutsch: German and English are siblings – both West Germanic. Many basic words are almost the same. The word decoder below explains why they still sound different.
sprachen.cmp.note: Being related helps with vocabulary – for grammar and pronunciation, practice is what counts.
sprachen.dec.title: German → English: the word decoder
sprachen.dec.lead: German and English are siblings: many words are really the same word. From around the 6th century German changed some sounds (the “High German consonant shift”); English kept the older ones. If you know German, these patterns help you guess English words.
sprachen.dec.step1: At the top is a sound swap: the German sound on the left, the English sound on the right.
sprachen.dec.step2: Below are examples: German word → English word.
sprachen.dec.step3: Try it with a German word you know: swap the sound back – often the English word comes out.
sprachen.dec.note: The first four patterns come from the consonant shift; the others are later changes. They're rules of thumb – not every word fits.

dialekte.title: Accents of English in the British Isles
dialekte.lead: From Scouse to Geordie: how English sounds in different parts of the UK and Ireland. Pick a region for examples and typical words, or see how people say hello and what they call a bread roll.
dialekte.map.title: The accent map
dialekte.map.lead: The colours show six big groups: the North of England, the Midlands, the South, Scotland, Wales and Ireland. The dots are well-known city accents and the Celtic languages.
dialekte.map.empty: Click a region or a dot on the map.
dialekte.map.wordNote: Simplified: in many places you hear several words, and the standard word is understood everywhere.
dialekte.group.north.text: Bus rhymes with push, and bath has a short a. Many words come from Old Norse.
dialekte.group.midlands.text: Between North and South: northern vowels (bus, bath), but a melody of its own.
dialekte.group.south.text: In much of the South bath has a long ah, and bus a short /ʌ/. Without an r in car – except in the West Country.
dialekte.group.scotland.text: The r is always pronounced. Many people also speak Scots, and some Scottish Gaelic.
dialekte.group.wales.text: English with a Welsh melody. Many people in the north and west speak Welsh first.
dialekte.group.ireland.text: The r is pronounced, th often sounds like t or d, and Irish shapes the grammar.
dialekte.r.northeast: Geordie is the accent of Tyneside; Mackem is the accent of Sunderland. Many words are old and close to Scots: bairn (child), gan (go), hyem (home). “Pet” and “hinny” are friendly ways to talk to someone.
dialekte.r.cumbria: Cumbrian English in the far north-west of England has many words from Old Norse, the language of the Vikings who settled here. Farmers in the Lake District once counted sheep with old numbers like yan, tyan, tethera.
dialekte.r.yorkshire: Yorkshire people are proud of their accent. Typical sounds: short a in bath and grass, bus rhymes with push, and the often becomes just t’ (“going t’ shop”). Hull has its own sound: “phone” can sound like “fern”.
dialekte.r.northwest: In Manchester people say “our kid” for a brother or sister and “dead good” for very good. Some older speakers in rural Lancashire still pronounce the r in car. Liverpool, at the western edge, has an accent of its own: Scouse (see the dot).
dialekte.r.westmidlands: The Black Country, west of Birmingham, keeps many old forms: “yow am” for you are – that is why people from there are nicknamed yam-yams. In the Potteries around Stoke-on-Trent, people call each other “duck”. Birmingham has its own dot: Brummie.
dialekte.r.eastmidlands: “Ey up, me duck” is the classic East Midlands greeting – “duck” is friendly, for anyone. Like in the North, bus rhymes with push and bath has a short a. Mardy (moody) is known all over England.
dialekte.r.eastanglia: In Norfolk you often hear “noo” for new and “Hoo” for Hugh: the y sound before u disappears. Verbs can drop the -s: “she like it”. The melody goes up and down a lot.
dialekte.r.southeast: Estuary English, between Cockney and standard southern English, has spread far beyond London: the t in “water” or “get it” becomes a stop in the throat, and l at the end of a word sounds like w (“miwk” for milk). This is close to the accent many textbooks use.
dialekte.r.southwest: The West Country is the only big part of England where many people still pronounce the r in car and farm. In Bristol, an l is often added at the end of words: “idea” can sound like “ideal”.
dialekte.r.lowlands: Here people speak Scottish English, and many also speak Scots, a sister language of English. The r is always pronounced, often rolled or tapped, and “loch” has the ch sound of German Bach. Glasgow has its own dot.
dialekte.r.northeastscotland: Doric is the Scots of Aberdeen and the North East. Its best-known feature: wh becomes f, so “fit” means what and “far” means where. “Fit like?” – “Nae bad” is a whole conversation.
dialekte.r.highlands: Highland English is often said to be soft and clear. Many families here once spoke Scottish Gaelic, and some still do, especially in the islands – so English here has a Gaelic melody and Gaelic words.
dialekte.r.northernisles: Until the 1700s many people here spoke Norn, a language close to Norwegian. The local Scots still has many Norse words, and Shetlanders say “du” to friends, like Norwegians. On the map, Shetland is shown in a box: it really lies further north.
dialekte.r.northmidwales: In the north and west of Wales, many people grow up speaking Welsh and learn English as a second language. Welsh English has the Welsh sing-song melody and some Welsh sentence patterns: “There’s lovely!”, “Coming tomorrow, is he?”
dialekte.r.southwales: Most people in the south speak English as their first language, but the Welsh melody stayed – “Wenglish”. “Now” does not always mean now: “I’ll do it now” can mean later. Cardiff’s own accent has a long, flat a: “Kairdiff”.
dialekte.r.ulster: Ulster English mixes Irish English with Scots, brought by settlers from Scotland in the 17th century. Statements often go up at the end, so they can sound like questions. Ulster Scots is spoken in parts of Antrim and Down. Belfast has its own dot.
dialekte.r.southirish: Irish English keeps patterns from Irish (Gaelic): “I’m after eating” means I have just eaten. The r is pronounced, and th often sounds like t or d: “tree” for three. Cork is known for its fast, sing-song accent.
dialekte.m.liverpool: Scouse sounds very different from the towns around it. A k or t can become a hissing sound in the throat: “back” sounds a bit like “bach”. The name comes from scouse, a stew of meat and potatoes.
dialekte.m.birmingham: Brummie has a falling melody that is easy to recognise, and “I” sounds close to “oy”. Birmingham is the UK’s second-largest city, and its accent is often heard on TV.
dialekte.m.london: Cockney is the old accent of the East End: “fink” for think, no h in “’ouse”, and rhyming slang. Today many young Londoners speak Multicultural London English (MLE), with words from Jamaican Patois, other languages and street slang.
dialekte.m.glasgow: Glaswegian is fast and full of Scots: “gonnae” (going to), “dinnae” (don’t), “wean” (child, from wee one). The t in the middle of a word often disappears into the throat: “wa’er” for water.
dialekte.m.belfast: In Belfast, “What about ye?” (often just “Bout ye?”) means hello. Belfast vowels sound very different from English accents, and many sentences go up at the end.
dialekte.m.dublin: Dublin English has its own words and a quick rhythm. Like everywhere in Ireland, people say “grand” for fine and use “ye” or “youse” for more than one person.
dialekte.m.welsh: Welsh (Cymraeg) is a Celtic language and an official language in Wales, next to English. Road signs and schools are bilingual, and in parts of the north and west most people speak Welsh at home.
dialekte.m.gaelic: Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language, related to Irish. It is strongest in the Outer Hebrides; many place names all over the Highlands come from Gaelic.
dialekte.m.irish: Irish (Gaeilge) is the first official language of Ireland. Everyone learns it at school, but it is the everyday language mainly in the Gaeltacht, areas in the west such as Connemara.
dialekte.m.cornish: Cornish (Kernewek) is a Celtic language related to Welsh and Breton. It stopped being spoken as an everyday language in the 18th century; today a small community has brought it back.
dialekte.m.manx: Manx (Gaelg) is the Celtic language of the Isle of Man, which is not part of the UK. Its last native speaker died in 1974; today children can learn it again at a Manx-language primary school.
dialekte.lines.title: Two lines divide England
dialekte.lines.lead: Two sound changes happened in the south of England from about the 17th century and never reached the north. The lines on the map show roughly where they stop – they run close together from the Welsh border to the Wash.
dialekte.lines.benrath.title: The bus line: /bʊs/ | /bʌs/
dialekte.lines.benrath.text: North of the line, bus, cup and love have the same vowel as push and put (/ʊ/). South of it, they have a different vowel (/ʌ/), so putt and put sound different. Linguists call this the FOOT–STRUT split.
dialekte.lines.speyer.title: The bath line: short a | long ah
dialekte.lines.speyer.text: North of the line, bath, grass and laugh have the same short a as cat. South of it, in much of the south-east, they have a long ah (/ɑː/), as in father. Linguists call this the TRAP–BATH split.
dialekte.lines.note: Simplified: inside every group there are many local accents, and younger speakers often sound different from older ones. Most phonetic signs here are rough guides.
dialekte.learn.title: Do I have to learn an accent?
dialekte.learn.text: No. Standard English is understood everywhere, and you need it for exams, school and work. But it helps to recognise a few accents and words from the place where you live: “Alright?”, “Ey up” or “Hiya” open many doors. If you move to a region with a strong accent, listening to local speakers is the best practice.
dialekte.src.title: Sources
dialekte.src.text: A simplified overview based on J. C. Wells, Accents of English (1982), the British Library’s “Sounds Familiar?” collection and the Wikipedia articles on the accents and languages named here (checked November 2026). Real accent borders are fluid; the areas and lines are drawn roughly. Map outlines: Natural Earth (public domain).

kl.d.explain.p1: Each exercise is scored in your students' browser, and only then does the browser send us the result; that is why it says “self-reported”. Anyone who can use developer tools can fake these numbers. Nobody can see whether someone helped or a dictionary was open.
kl.d.explain.p2: Here you see who practises how much and which topics cause trouble. That is not enough for grades. The live quiz you run yourself in class measures more reliably.
kl.d.explain.p3: Hints about pasted text, tab switches and very fast answers are only counted and change no result. They can be harmless, for example a word pasted from one's own notes or a message answered quickly.
kl.d.explain.p4: Minutes count from the first to the last answer of an exercise; reading time before that is not included.

satzmelodie.task1.title: Listen and compare the melody.
satzmelodie.task1.text: Repeat after me: after each sentence you have time to say it out loud. With the microphone 🎤 next to a sentence you can check your own melody – the recording stays on your device.
satzmelodie.caveat: Careful, echo question ↗↗: in Spanish, “¿Ana viene mañana?” and “Ana viene mañana.” have the same words, so the melody is what makes it a question. A normal yes/no question rises a little. An echo question rises much higher, and it means something different: you're surprised or checking that you heard right (“¿Que viene mañana?”).

satzmelodie.task2.title: Listen. Statement, question or exclamation?
satzmelodie.task2.text: The words are always the same. Only the melody is different. Add the punctuation marks.

satzmelodie.task3.text: The answer is always the same sentence. The question decides which word gets the stress.
satzmelodie.task4.title: Melody maze: which exit?
satzmelodie.task4.text: Quaki hops through the sentence with the voice. At the end the path splits: does the voice go up, down, or steeply down? Then you see the real melody – and Quaki rides along it.
satzmelodie.lab.aria: Maze: at the end of the sentence the path splits into three exits – top: question, bottom: statement, very bottom: exclamation.
satzmelodie.rule.title: The melody at the end of the sentence
satzmelodie.rule.aussage: The voice falls at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.w: The voice usually falls at the end, as in a statement. Questions with qué, dónde, cuándo, quién, cómo, por qué, cuánto and cuál. With a gentle rise instead, they sound extra friendly.
satzmelodie.rule.jn: Often the same words as a statement: only the melody, and ¿ ? in writing, makes it a question. The voice rises at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.echo: The voice rises high at the end. You're surprised or checking what you heard. Spanish often starts it with que.
satzmelodie.rule.ausruf: The stressed word goes very high, then the voice falls a long way. Feeling: joy, anger, surprise.
satzmelodie.rule.liste: The voice stays level → until the list is finished. Then it falls ↘.
satzmelodie.teacherTip: For teachers: a pair activity with three cards (. ? !). A says “Ana viene mañana” with one melody, B holds up the matching card.

satzmelodie.why.ausruf: Exclamation: the voice starts high and falls sharply ↘. You're excited or surprised.

wissen.lernen.lead: Mistakes are allowed. Even more: without mistakes you learn more slowly. Here Bruno, Regi, Hamsti and Quaki explain how your brain really holds on to Spanish.
wissen.lernen.jungle.title: Your brain is a jungle
wissen.lernen.jungle.lead: Imagine this: a new word lies on the other side of a dense jungle. There's no path to it yet. You have to cut it yourself.
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.title: The machete
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.text: Learning is your machete. On your first try you hack your way through the jungle with effort. That's tiring – and completely normal.
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.title: The wrong way
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.text: Sometimes you walk in the wrong direction: a mistake. Your brain notices the difference between what it expected and the right answer. That very signal shows it where the path really goes.
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.title: The beaten path
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.text: Every time you walk the path again, it gets wider. Nerve cells that often work together connect more strongly.
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.title: The road
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.text: After many repetitions the path has become a road. You don't have to think anymore – the word is just there. Practice even changes the wiring in your brain along the way.
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot1: And a path you don't walk for a long time? It slowly grows over again. That's why you repeat (Rule 3).
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot2: Your brain constantly rebuilding itself like this is called neuroplasticity. Adults who learn to juggle for three months have measurably more grey matter afterwards
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot4: And London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot5: Your brain learns at any age.
wissen.lernen.wheel.label: The seven rules
wissen.lernen.wheel.title: The learning circle
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.title: Making mistakes is part of it
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.text: You're not supposed to get everything right straight away. If you try an answer, get it wrong and then see the right one, you remember it better than if you only read it.
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.why: A mistake surprises your brain. That surprise makes the correction stick. Even mistakes you were completely sure about get corrected especially well afterwards. The only important thing: always look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.say: Hmm … what was it called again?
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.title: Recall first, then check
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.text: Reading a word list five times feels good – but doesn't do much. Better: cover the word and quiz yourself. Only then do you check.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.why: Every time you pull a word out of your head, the path to it gets wider. Reading only goes through your eyes. Remembering is work, and that very work is what stays.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.title: A little, but often – and sleep well
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.text: Ten minutes every day are better than two hours on Sunday. And when you've almost forgotten a word, that's the best moment to review it.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.why: With breaks between reviews, knowledge stays much longer. While you sleep, your brain sorts what you learned during the day. So learning in the evening and a quick review in the morning go well together.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.title: Mix instead of blocks
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.text: Twenty sentences with only the present tense are easy – you already know what's coming. In real life you don't. So mix it up: present, past and future, all jumbled.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.why: When you mix, you learn not only the rule but also when you need it. That's harder, but it's exactly what you need in conversation and in the exam.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.title: Speak out loud, don't just read
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.text: Read new sentences out loud. Speak along when you listen to audio. Even alone in the kitchen – that's not weird, that's training.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.why: What you say out loud, you also hear, and you move your mouth while doing it. So your head remembers the sentence in several ways. And your mouth learns the words before you need them in a conversation.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.title: It can be hard – but not too hard
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.text: If everything is easy, you learn little. If everything is too hard, you give up. You learn the most in between: you have to think, but you usually manage.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.why: The effort isn't a sign that you're bad at it. It's the sign that you're learning right now. Choose your level so that you get about eight out of ten tasks right.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.title: Celebrate small steps
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.text: Don't compare yourself with others. Compare yourself with yourself a month ago. Every new word is a step.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.why: Anyone who sees their progress keeps learning. Small goals that you really reach keep you going longer than one big goal that's far away.
wissen.lernen.sum.title: In short
wissen.lernen.sum.1: Try it yourself first – even if you get it wrong.
wissen.lernen.sum.2: After every mistake, look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.sum.3: Better a little every day than a lot once.
wissen.lernen.sum.4: Mix the topics and speak out loud.
wissen.lernen.studies.title: The studies
wissen.lernen.studies.lead: The asterisks (*) in the text lead here. The studies are in English.
wissen.lernen.study.schultz: The brain signals the difference between expectation and outcome – this error signal steers learning.
wissen.lernen.study.rumelhart: Artificial neural networks learn by correcting their connections a little after every error.
wissen.lernen.study.hebb: Nerve cells that are often active at the same time connect more strongly – the basic idea behind the “beaten path”.
wissen.lernen.study.bengtsson: A lot of practice changes the nerve pathways themselves (the white matter).
wissen.lernen.study.draganski: After three months of juggling, adults' grey matter grew – and shrank back when they stopped.
wissen.lernen.study.boyke: The same works for people around 60, too.
wissen.lernen.study.maguire: London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus – the longer in the job, the clearer it is.
wissen.lernen.study.kornell: Guessing wrong first and then seeing the answer helps more than reading the answer straight away.
wissen.lernen.study.butterfield: Mistakes you were sure about are remembered especially well after they are corrected.
wissen.lernen.study.metcalfe: Overview: mistakes that get corrected help learning instead of harming it.
wissen.lernen.study.roediger: Quizzing yourself keeps knowledge longer than reading it again.
wissen.lernen.study.cepeda: Reviewing with breaks in between beats learning in one go.
wissen.lernen.study.rasch: During sleep the brain consolidates what was learned during the day.
wissen.lernen.study.rohrer: Mixed tasks did clearly better in the later test than tasks in blocks.
wissen.lernen.study.macleod: Words read aloud are remembered better than words read silently.
wissen.lernen.study.bjork: “Desirable difficulties”: what feels hard while practising often stays longer.
wissen.lernen.study.wilson: Learning models make the fastest progress when they get about 85% of the tasks right.

wortfallen.lead: Some words look like a word you already know, or almost like another Spanish word, and mean something completely different. Here are {n} traps, each with a memory trick.
wortfallen.embarazada.react: Pregnant? Congratulations! But what does your boss have to do with it?
wortfallen.embarazada.tip: False friend for English speakers, and for Portuguese (embaraçada), Italian (imbarazzata) and French (embarrassée) speakers too. embarazada only means pregnant. Embarrassed: avergonzado/a, or just ¡Qué vergüenza!
wortfallen.constipado.react: A cold? Then why are you talking about the toilet?
wortfallen.constipado.tip: False friend for English and French speakers (constipé). In Spain, constipado means you have a cold: the nose, not the stomach. At the doctor's, this one matters.
wortfallen.exito.react: Success? We're all looking for that!
wortfallen.exito.tip: False friend for English speakers. éxito is success: la película fue un éxito. On the door and on the metro signs you'll read SALIDA.
wortfallen.carpeta.react: A new folder? On the floor? Your papers must be very tidy.
wortfallen.carpeta.tip: False friend for English speakers (carpet) and French speakers (carpette). Keep your NIE papers in a carpeta. You walk on an alfombra.
wortfallen.libreria.react: For free? The bookseller won't be happy about that!
wortfallen.libreria.tip: False friend for English speakers. A library is la biblioteca, and you borrow from it. In a librería you pay. French librairie and Italian libreria work like the Spanish word.
wortfallen.actualmente.react: So you're not from Madrid right now? Where will you be from tomorrow?
wortfallen.actualmente.tip: False friend for English speakers. actualmente = now. Actually = en realidad or la verdad es que. It's the same with actual: el precio actual is today's price.
wortfallen.sensible.react: Sensitive? Does she cry at her bank statements?
wortfallen.sensible.tip: False friend for English speakers. sensible means sensitive, like a person who cries at films or skin that burns easily. Sensible, with good judgement, is sensato/a.
wortfallen.realizar.react: You carried it out? So you lost your keys on purpose?
wortfallen.realizar.tip: False friend for English speakers. realizar = to carry out: realizar un pago, realizar una obra. To realise = darse cuenta de: me doy cuenta de que …
wortfallen.gimnasio.react: She does her maths on the treadmill?
wortfallen.gimnasio.tip: False friend for German speakers: das Gymnasium = el instituto, a public secondary school in Spain. el gimnasio is where you lift weights.
wortfallen.tasa.react: A coffee fee? The tax office would love that!
wortfallen.tasa.tip: False friend for German speakers: die Tasse = la taza, with z. You pay una tasa at the office, for example to renew a document. In most of Spain the two words sound different: tasa with s, taza with the th of think.
wortfallen.mantel.react: The tablecloth? You'll have lunch on your shoulders!
wortfallen.mantel.tip: False friend for German speakers: der Mantel = el abrigo. el mantel goes on the table before a meal.
wortfallen.regalo.react: All your books in one present? Who's the lucky person?
wortfallen.regalo.tip: False friend for German speakers: das Regal = la estantería. el regalo is a present, the thing you give on a birthday.
wortfallen.largo.react: Long? Then the cars must be parked one after another.
wortfallen.largo.tip: False friend for French speakers (large), and also for Italian and Portuguese speakers (largo) and Romanian speakers (larg): all of them mean wide. In Spanish, largo is long; wide is ancho.
wortfallen.atender.react: You're serving the bus? Would it like a coffee?
wortfallen.atender.tip: False friend for French speakers: attendre = esperar. atender is what staff do: el médico atiende a los pacientes. English speakers beware as well: to attend a class is asistir a clase.
wortfallen.quitar.react: You removed France? Does the map know?
wortfallen.quitar.tip: False friend for French speakers: quitter = dejar or irse de. quitar is to take something away: quitar una mancha.
wortfallen.exquisito.tip: False friend for Portuguese speakers: esquisito = raro. exquisito is high praise, usually for food: la paella está exquisita.
wortfallen.polvo.react: A plate of dust, Galician style? Is that a house special?
wortfallen.polvo.tip: False friend for Portuguese speakers: polvo = el pulpo. In Spanish, el polvo is dust. Take extra care: echar un polvo is slang for having sex.
wortfallen.oficina.react: To the office? Does it have an appointment with the boss?
wortfallen.oficina.tip: False friend for Portuguese speakers: oficina = el taller. la oficina in Spanish is where you sit at a desk.
wortfallen.borracha.react: A drunk woman? To fix your spelling?
wortfallen.borracha.tip: False friend for Portuguese speakers: borracha = la goma. In Spanish, borracho/a means someone who has drunk too much.
wortfallen.burro.react: Bread with donkey? That's a tapa I don't know!
wortfallen.burro.tip: False friend for Italian speakers: il burro = la mantequilla. el burro is the animal, and also a mild insult for someone stubborn.
wortfallen.salir.react: You're going out to the third floor? Through the window?
wortfallen.salir.tip: False friend for Italian speakers: salire = subir. salir is to go out: salgo de casa a las ocho.
wortfallen.guardar.react: You put the TV away every night? In the wardrobe?
wortfallen.guardar.tip: False friend for Italian speakers: guardare = ver or mirar. In Spanish, guardar means to keep something safe: guarda el pasaporte.
wortfallen.cansado.react: Very married? Does your wife know about the twelve hours?
wortfallen.cansado.tip: Only one letter apart: cansado has an n, as in no sleep. Both go with estar: estoy cansado, estoy casado.
wortfallen.hambre.react: You have a lot of men? And you want to eat now?
wortfallen.hambre.tip: hambre starts like hamburguesa. hombre is a man. Careful: we say el hambre, but the word is feminine, so it's mucha hambre.
wortfallen.pero.react: You want to go, dog? You can't? Who's talking to the dog?
wortfallen.pero.tip: One r is one quick tap; rr is several. Say them aloud: pero, perro. The difference is in your tongue, and you can practise it on the pronunciation page.

verben.group.regelmaessig.name: Regular verbs

verben.group.trennbar.name: Reflexive and pronominal verbs
